title: Geometric stalks commute with etale-to-pro-etale inverse image
statement:
Let $T$ be a scheme, $\bar t:\operatorname{Spec}\Omega\to T$ a geometric point [def-weil-geometric-point], and $\nu_T:T_{\mathrm{proet}}\to T_{\mathrm{et}}$ the comparison geometric morphism [def-weil-pbc-site-comparison-morphism]. For every sheaf $\mathcal H$ of sets or abelian groups on the small etale site, there is a canonical isomorphism
$$(\nu_T^*\mathcal H)_{\bar t}\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathcal H_{\bar t},$$
natural in $\mathcal H$. The left stalk is defined using pointed weakly etale neighbourhoods [def-weil-proetale-geometric-stalk], and the right stalk using pointed etale neighbourhoods [def-weil-pbc-geometric-stalks]. In the abelian case the isomorphism is additive. If $\mathcal H$ is a sheaf of left modules over a fixed ring $\Lambda$, where comparison inverse image on these modules means applying the set inverse image to the underlying sheaf and its addition, zero, negation and each scalar operation, it is $\Lambda$-linear; commutativity and finiteness of $\Lambda$ are not required.

proof.text: Put $C=A^{\mathrm{sh}}_{T,\bar t}$ and $S=\operatorname{Spec}C=T_{(\bar t)}$ with structural map $p:S\to T$. The local-structure lemma gives a local-ring structure on $C$ for which $C$ is strictly henselian. Apply the pointed-map lemma with this structure: it gives $\psi:C\twoheadrightarrow K\subset\Omega$ with kernel the maximal ideal and with the specified neighbourhood projection equations. The composite $C\to K\hookrightarrow\Omega$ defines $\bar s:\operatorname{Spec}\Omega\to S$. Its image is the closed point because the kernel is the maximal ideal. The projection equations and the definition of the structural map give $p\bar s=\bar t$. Thus the strictly henselian sections lemma can be applied at $\bar s$, rather than at an arbitrary point of $S$.

proof.text: By the classical pro-etale stalk lemma, $S\to T$ is an object of the pro-etale site and the germ map $(\nu_T^*H)(S)\to(\nu_T^*H)_{\bar t}$ is a canonical isomorphism, natural in the sheaf $H$. Use its inverse to start the desired comparison. This is an evaluation formula on the strict localization; it does not assert that etale neighbourhoods are cofinal among weakly etale neighbourhoods.

Apply the sections formula to the object $p:S\to T$. It identifies $(\nu_T^*H)(S)$ with $\Gamma(S_{\mathrm{et}},p_{\mathrm{et}}^{-1}H)$, naturally in $H$. Since Step 2 places $p$ in the pro-etale site, the weakly etale hypothesis of that formula is satisfied. The identification is with the ordinary inverse image of sheaves of sets, with no tensor product or change of coefficient ring.

Apply the sets version of the strictly henselian sections lemma with its ambient scheme and open subscheme both equal to $S$. Step 1 gives precisely its hypotheses: a strictly henselian local coordinate ring and a geometric point at the closed point. Its germ map identifies $\Gamma(S_{\mathrm{et}},p_{\mathrm{et}}^{-1}H)$ with $(p_{\mathrm{et}}^{-1}H)_{\bar s}$. Apply the etale inverse-image stalk-germ lemma to $p$ and $\bar s$; since $p\bar s=\bar t$, this last stalk is bijective to $H_{\bar t}$. Composing these bijections with Steps 2 and 3 defines $c_H:(\nu_T^*H)_{\bar t}\xrightarrow{\sim}H_{\bar t}$.

The evaluations and germ maps in the first three arrows of this composite commute with a sheaf morphism $a:H\to H'$ (evaluation and germ are componentwise, and the sections formula is natural). For the last arrow, apply the characterization in the stalk-germ lemma to a pulled-back section $s\in H(U)$: either composite with $a$ sends its germ to the germ of $a_U(s)$. Naturality of the inverse-image unit is the clause (0) of the composition-units lemma. These pulled-back germs exhaust the source stalk: an element maps under the bijection of Step 4 to a germ represented by a section of H on a pointed etale neighbourhood; the pulled-back germ of that section has the same image, so injectivity makes it the original element. The two composites are therefore equal on every element. This uses the bijection and its formula on unit germs, not a uniqueness assertion for a different codomain. This proves $c_{H'}(\nu_T^*a)_{\bar t}=a_{\bar t}c_H$. All choices in Step 1 give the same $\bar s$: its composites with every limit projection are the specified lifts, so the inverse-limit universal property determines it. Hence the isomorphism is canonical, not dependent on a chosen local-ring structure or presentation.

proof.text: Write $P(H)=(\nu_T^*H)_{\bar t}$ and $Q(H)=H_{\bar t}$ for the two functors on etale sheaves of sets. $P$ preserves finite products: comparison inverse image preserves finite limits by the geometric-morphism definition, and the classical stalk identification makes the second functor evaluation at $S$, which preserves sectionwise products and the terminal sheaf. The etale stalk finite-limits lemma gives the same assertion for $Q$. Under these product identifications, naturality from Step 5 with the two projections gives $c_{H\times H}(x,y)=(c_H(x),c_H(y))$; on the terminal sheaf the component is the unique map. An abelian sheaf is an abelian group object, so naturality with $+:H\times H\to H$, $0:*\to H$, and negation gives $c_H(x+y)=c_H(x)+c_H(y)$, $c_H(0)=0$, and $c_H(-x)=-c_H(x)$. The inverse bijection is additive as well. On abelian sheaves this is the asserted abelian stalk isomorphism: the two pointed-neighbourhood colimits are filtered, and forgetting abelian groups preserves filtered colimits. Thus their underlying sets are exactly the stalks used in Steps 2--5. The identification of abelian comparison inverse image with the set inverse image equipped with its group operations is clause (3) of [def-weil-pbc-sites-and-cohomology], so the abelian functor here is the one in the statement.

proof.text: For a sheaf of left $\Lambda$-modules, the inverse image in the statement applies the set functor to each scalar endomorphism $\lambda_r:H\to H$ separately. Step 5 applied to $\lambda_r$ therefore gives $c_H(rx)=r c_H(x)$ for every $r\in\Lambda$; Step 6 supplies additivity. The filtered-module-colimit elementwise lemma identifies these stalk structures with module colimits: every element has a section representative, equality holds after a common refinement, and the operations are $[x]+[y]=[x|_W+y|_W]$, $r[x]=[rx]$ on a common pointed refinement $W$. These formulas are well defined because restrictions are linear, and have the module-colimit universal property since a compatible family of linear maps preserves the displayed operations. Consequently the comparison and its inverse are $\Lambda$-linear. This argument uses only a fixed ring and each individual scalar operation, so neither commutativity nor finiteness of $\Lambda$ is needed.
